title: Planting forests
hookLine: Sikh groups plant small forests to honor Guru Nanak

cards: A scrap of land behind a village school: hard dirt, a broken wall, a pile of bricks nobody moved.
A sangat arrives after the Sunday program with saplings in plastic bags, a cart of compost, and a list of trees that belong to this soil. They don't plant in neat rows.
They plant close, shoulder to shoulder, the way a real forest grows, and children press the earth down around each stem. A few seasons later, that scrap of dirt is a green wall full of birds.
It was planted for one person.

teach.b: Sikh groups have been planting small, dense forests in honor of Guru Nanak, on patches of land near gurdwaras, schools, farms and villages. Some call them Guru Nanak sacred forests.
Instead of a few big trees far apart, they plant native trees and shrubs close together, so they compete for light and grow fast and thick. Some groups use a way of planting that comes from Japan.

The point is a real forest on a small plot, not a park. The root is a short salok at Ang 8, which Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning say at its end. In Gurmukhi it begins: pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat.

teach.h: AIR GURU, WATER FATHER, EARTH MOTHER.
teach.b: Air is the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. So a forest isn't decoration. It's family: the ones the salok names as teacher and parents.
There's an old green thread, too.

Tradition remembers Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, keeping gardens and growing healing herbs, and tells of him as a boy brushing a flower with his robe and breaking it, and taking care with every living thing after that.
The forests carry that thread forward.
A tree planted for Nanak gives shade to anyone, of any faith, who sits under it, and gives the great mother back a little of what was taken.

how: Some Sikh organizations and sangats plant small, dense forests of native trees near gurdwaras, schools and villages in honor of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs recite the Japji's closing salok, which names air, water and earth as Guru, father and mother.

games.q: there's a scrap of hard dirt behind your gurdwara, full of bricks. the sangat wants to honor Guru Nanak. what does today's story point to?

put up a plaque and leave the dirt.
games.why: Sikh groups turn scraps like this into small, dense forests for Guru Nanak, a family of air, water and earth.

practice: Breathe in and notice the air, the Guru, the salok says; feel your feet on the floor and the earth below it, the great mother; think of the water inside you, the father. Stay with whichever one is easiest to feel.
If you pray, you can say pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat once, slowly.
